title: MTRX™ Field Series No. 00 · The learning operating system · Kevin Cecil

cards.name: Why Field Guide 01 had gaps, and what changed
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why Field Guide 01 had gaps, and what changed" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Coverage is the guide's job. Understanding is mine. Recall a week later is the only receipt."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Why reading everything still feels empty
cards.q: You finish a stop, it felt crystal clear, and you rate yourself 5 out of 5 immediately. What is the problem?
options: Immediate ratings run on fluency, so they overestimate; rate later and test
You should reread it twice more
5 out of 5 is fine if the topic is easy
cards.why: Ratings made right after reading track how smooth it felt. Ratings made after a delay track what you can actually retrieve. Delay the judgment, then test it.

cards.name: Why reading everything still feels empty
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why reading everything still feels empty" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't trust the feeling of getting it. I trust what I can explain tomorrow with the page closed."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The principles that survived the evidence
cards.q: Productive failure (struggling before instruction) works best for which kind of learning?
cards.why: Sinha and Kapur found a moderate gain for conceptual knowledge and transfer and roughly zero for procedural skill. Struggle first on "why", get shown on "how".

cards.name: The principles that survived the evidence
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The principles that survived the evidence" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Input is necessary. Output is where it sticks."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Myths to drop
cards.q: Which of these is NOT supported by evidence?
options: Matching lessons to your learning style
Explaining a concept with the page closed
cards.why: The style-matching claim needs a specific interaction effect that has not been shown. The other three are among the best-supported methods there are.

cards.name: Myths to drop
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Myths to drop" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Learning styles are a preference, not a mechanism. I use words and diagrams, and I test myself."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Why you cannot just ask "what am I missing?"
cards.q: What is the most reliable way to find concepts you have never heard of?
options: Ask one expert to list everything
Read more of your favourite source
Overlay 5+ independent sources (syllabi, certifications, docs) and diff them against what you know
Wait until a client mentions it
cards.why: Each source has blind spots, but independent sources have different ones. Where they overlap is the core; where one has something the others lack is a candidate gap to check.

cards.name: Why you cannot just ask "what am I missing?"
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why you cannot just ask "what am I missing?"" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Nobody can list what they don't know. So I don't list, I diff against syllabi."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The 12-step protocol
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The 12-step protocol" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't write a guide until the map has been diffed against five independent sources and hunted five ways for gaps."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The 13 lenses: questions for any field
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The 13 lenses: questions for any field" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Any field answers the same 13 questions. The ones I can't answer are my syllabus."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Sources, tiers and the T-shape
cards.q: A concept appears in your guide's glossary but nowhere in the lessons. In the coverage audit it counts as:
options: A gap candidate: mentioned, not explained
cards.why: Glossary-only means you might recognise the word but have never seen the mechanism. That is exactly the fluency trap. The audit only counts body-text explanations.

cards.name: Sources, tiers and the T-shape
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Sources, tiers and the T-shape" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Wide on the map, deep on the spine that pays."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The daily 20
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The daily 20" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Eight minutes in, twelve minutes out. That ratio is the whole trick."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Week, month, quarter
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Week, month, quarter" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "The day keeps it alive. The week makes me teach it. The month tells me the truth."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Know that you know
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Know that you know" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I know which of my opinions are earned and which are borrowed."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Try-it rule
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Try-it rule" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Whenever a client says 'remember me', I hear cookies, sessions and consent."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Your weak-spot log
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Your weak-spot log" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "My misses are my syllabus."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Your two quotes, unlearned
cards.q: Who actually wrote the phrase "learn, unlearn and relearn"?
cards.why: Toffler wrote the phrase; the "illiterate" part is psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy, quoted by Toffler. The polished one-liner is a later blend.

cards.name: Your two quotes, unlearned
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Your two quotes, unlearned" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Toffler said learn, unlearn, relearn. Darwin's real trick was writing down what contradicted him."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Curiosity, the ignition
cards.q: Which design best uses curiosity in a lesson?
options: Open with a funny unrelated story
Pose a specific puzzle, ask for a guess with confidence, then explain the mechanism promptly
Hide the answer until the very end of the guide
Add lots of surprising facts throughout
cards.why: A visible, solvable gap plus a committed guess, closed quickly by the core idea. Unrelated stories and scattered facts are seductive details; hiding answers is clickbait.

cards.name: Curiosity, the ignition
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Curiosity, the ignition" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Curiosity is the ignition. Retrieval is the engine."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: How to unlearn
cards.q: You correct a belief by noting "X is false" but give no alternative explanation. What usually happens?
options: The old belief keeps influencing you, because nothing replaced it
cards.why: The continued influence effect: a correction without a replacement model leaves a gap, and the old explanation keeps filling it.

cards.name: How to unlearn
cards.q: Page closed: explain "How to unlearn" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "What would make me drop this belief? If I can't answer, I'm not holding it, it's holding me."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Any age, honestly
cards.q: Which kind of activity improved older adults' memory in the Synapse Project?
options: Sustained practice at demanding new skills
cards.why: Novel, demanding, sustained practice. The lesson for any age: keep picking things that are hard and new for you, and stick with them for months.

cards.name: Any age, honestly
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Any age, honestly" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "Speed peaks early. Knowledge compounds. I'm building the part that compounds."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Mental strength that actually works
cards.q: Which tactic has the strongest evidence for turning a learning goal into daily action?
options: A specific if-then plan tied to a daily cue
cards.why: Implementation intentions: about d = 0.65 across 94 tests. They hand the decision to a cue, so you don't have to rely on willpower or mood.

cards.name: Mental strength that actually works
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Mental strength that actually works" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't rely on willpower. I rely on a cue, a plan, and never missing twice."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: How I think when I build a guide
cards.q: Page closed: explain "How I think when I build a guide" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "I don't trust my sense of completeness. I measure it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Where I can still fail
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Where I can still fail" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "The system catches errors. It doesn't pretend there are none."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The deal
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The deal" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "The guide gets better every month because my mistakes feed it."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The road ahead
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The road ahead" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: "One field at a time, mapped before it's taught."
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The system, tested
cards.q: The tech guide audit shows 320 of 320 must-know concepts covered. What does that prove?
options: You now understand all of tech
Every must-know concept from 14 sources is explained in the guide, nothing more
There are no gaps left anywhere
cards.why: Coverage is about the guide. Understanding is tested by your delayed recall. Unknown unknowns shrink, they never hit zero.

cards.name: The system, tested
cards.q: Why is the weekly teach-back done with no notes?
options: Retrieval is the learning, and gaps only show when nothing is in front of you
Notes are banned in the system
cards.why: With notes you are reading aloud, which is fluency again. Without them, every stumble marks a missing link.

cards.name: The system, tested
cards.q: A concept keeps coming back in your weak-spot log as "knew it, could not apply it". Best fix?
options: Add a new-surface case, a non-example and a cue, then apply it to a real client
cards.why: That is inert knowledge. The fix is transfer practice, not more input.
